tldr: AIPatient is an LLM-based simulated patient system using six AI agents and a Reasoning RAG framework with a knowledge graph built from MIMIC-III data, achieving 94.15% QA accuracy and demonstrating potential to transform medical education by matching or exceeding human-simulated patients.
contributions: Development of AIPatient, a simulated patient system powered by LLM-based AI agents with a Reasoning RAG agentic workflow
Construction of AIPatient Knowledge Graph from 1,500 deidentified patient records from MIMIC-III database
Comprehensive evaluation across QA accuracy, readability, robustness, stability, and clinical utility
Paired crossover user study comparing AIPatient with human-simulated patients in medical history taking
methods: The researchers developed AIPatient using six task-specific LLM-based AI agents in a Reasoning Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework. The AIPatient Knowledge Graph was constructed from 1,500 sampled patient records from MIMIC-III using LLM-based Named Entity Recognition, resulting in 15,441 nodes and 26,882 edges stored in Neo4j. Evaluation included ablation studies for QA accuracy across agent configurations, readability metrics (Flesch Reading Ease and Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level), robustness testing via question paraphrasing with ANOVA, stability assessment across 32 personality types, and a paired crossover user study with 20 medical students comparing AIPatient against human-simulated patients.
results: AIPatient achieved 94.15% QA accuracy with all six agents, surpassing benchmarks with partial or no agent integration. Knowledgebase validity reached F1=0.89 with GPT-4-Turbo. Readability scores showed median Flesch Reading Ease of 68.77 and median Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level of 6.4. Robustness was confirmed with non-significant variance (ANOVA F-value=0.6126, p>0.1). Stability showed median data loss of 2% across 32 personality types with no significant differences (F-value=0.782, p>0.1). The user study demonstrated AIPatient delivered high fidelity, usability, and educational value matching or exceeding human-simulated patients.
limitations: Current simulated patient systems face unresolved concerns about effectiveness and trustworthiness. Traditional evaluation often relies on subjective usability assessments and inter-rater reliability methods that are less generalizable. Variations in medical students' familiarity with simulated patient systems could cause inaccuracy in evaluation. The system showed significantly affected accuracy in Medical History category during robustness testing (F=5.3038, p=0.00589). Open-source models generally underperformed compared to commercial counterparts.
